title: Edge ML: Latency and Privacy
summary: Calculate aggregate sensor bandwidth demand and compare it against uplink limits to diagnose when edge processing is mandatory.

sections: The data locality invariant: When the network is too slow

blocks.md:
This lesson follows **Edge ML: Latency and Privacy** in *System Paradigms* (Vol I). By the end you should be able to:

- Calculate aggregate sensor bandwidth demand and compare it against uplink limits to diagnose when edge processing is mandatory
- Apply the data locality invariant equation to determine whether an application must run locally at the edge
- Evaluate why high-bandwidth cellular networks (5G/6G) cannot eliminate the need for edge ML in sub-10 ms control loops
- Calculate sustained accelerator requirements for edge deployments using hardware derating factors
- Evaluate the control loop timing constraints governing real-time industrial IoT ML deployments

blocks.source: Vol I, System Paradigms, § Edge ML: Latency and Privacy
blocks.md: The robotic-arm safety monitor in napkin math \ref{nbk-ml-systems-distance-penalty}, an industrial IoT (IIoT) control loop, left one option open: running the model beside the arm it protects. Edge ML is built on that move, trading elastic cloud capacity for shorter request paths and local data retention.

blocks.title: Map of the section
blocks.md:
The section is organised as:

- The data locality invariant: When the network is too slow
- Edge ML deployment challenges

Pay attention to: Bandwidth bottleneck in local sensor aggregation vs. cloud streaming; The data locality invariant and remote deadline feasibility testing; Edge accelerator sizing, hardware derating, and real-time industrial IoT.

blocks.prompt: Think first: Why cannot high-bandwidth wireless networking technologies (such as 5G or 6G) eliminate the need for edge ML in tight real-time control loops ($<10\text{ ms}$)?
blocks.md: While 5G and 6G technologies dramatically increase network bandwidth ($\text{BW}_{\text{network}}$) and reduce data transmission serialization time, they cannot alter the speed of light in optical fiber or eliminate physical geographic routing delays and protocol overhead ($L_{\text{lat,network}}$). For tight real-time control loops ($<10\text{ ms}$), physical round-trip propagation over geographic distances alone can consume the entire latency budget before any computation begins, making local edge execution physically mandatory.

questions.q: A manufacturing facility deploys 100 cameras recording uncompressed 1080p video (\$1920 × 1080 × 3 bytes/pixel) at 30 FPS. The factory has a dedicated 10 Gbps (~1.25 GB/s) fiber uplink. Why is streaming all raw video to a cloud ML server physically impossible?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is C. Each camera produces about \$1920 \times 1080 \times 3 \times 30 \approx 186.6\text{ MB/s}$, and multiplying by 100 cameras gives about \$18.66\text{ GB/s}$. The 10 Gbps uplink delivers only about \$1.25\text{ GB/s}$, so the raw stream is roughly \$15\times$ larger than the available link. The per-camera answer fails to multiply by all 100 cameras, the gigabits-versus-gigabytes answer compares unlike units without converting, and the compression answer assumes a reduction mechanism the scenario never grants. The physical impossibility here is for uncompressed raw streaming under the stated link budget.
questions.hint: Think about: calculate aggregate sensor bandwidth demand and compare it against uplink limits to diagnose when edge processing is mandatory.
options: The total is only about \$186.6 MB/s because that is the per-camera rate, so the 10 Gbps uplink has ample headroom.
The aggregate is about \$18.7 Gb/s because the camera output should be compared numerically to 10 Gbps without converting bytes to bits, so the link is close enough to be practical.
The aggregate raw video data rate is approximately \$18.7 GB/s, which exceeds the \$1.25 GB/s uplink capacity by roughly \$15×.
The aggregate raw stream is large, but normal compression assumptions would make it fit within the 10 Gbps uplink in practice.

questions.q: An autonomous drone navigates at 60 FPS (16.7 ms per-frame budget) capturing uncompressed 4K frames (~24.9 MB per frame). The drone connects via a 100 Mbps uplink to a cloud server whose round-trip latency plus inference time is 110 ms. Applying the data locality invariant, what is the feasibility of offloading this obstacle avoidance system to the cloud?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is D. Under the data locality screen, the remote-path lower-bound estimate is RemotePathTime ge fracDataVolumeNetworkBandwidth + NetworkLatency + fracOperationsRemotePeakRate × RemoteHardwareEfficiency. Transmitting \$24.9 MB = 199.2 Mbits over a \$100 Mbps uplink requires frac199.2100 approx 1.992 s approx 2,000 ms. Adding the 110 ms network/compute delay yields RemotePathTime approx 1,992 + 110 approx 2,100 ms, vastly exceeding the 16.7 ms per-frame budget. Because transmission time alone exceeds the deadline, this raw-frame offload is infeasible. A lower-bound estimate below the deadline would instead require complete-path measurement, including remote memory movement, queues, preprocessing, runtime overhead, and response serialization. The options claiming feasibility ignore the two-second transmission bottleneck. The option blaming telemetry protocols misses the fundamental bandwidth-latency physics.
questions.hint: Think about: apply the data locality invariant equation to determine whether an application must run locally at the edge.
options: Feasible, because the cloud GPU computes inference in under 10 ms.
Feasible, provided 5G network slicing is enabled on the drone modem.
Infeasible, solely because cloud servers do not support drone telemetry protocols.

Infeasible, because transmitting a 24.9 MB frame over a 100 Mbps link requires ~2,000 ms, causing even the remote-path lower-bound estimate (~2,100 ms) to violate the 16.7 ms frame deadline by over two orders of magnitude.

blocks.prompt: Explain it: A retail store needs about 5.2 TOPS of sustained throughput. Why does the chapter's estimate call for three 4 TOPS boards rather than two, even though two boards' combined 8 TOPS peak exceeds the target?
blocks.md: Hardware datasheets publish peak theoretical throughput ($R_{\text{peak}}$), but real-world sustained workloads encounter thermal limits, memory bandwidth bottlenecks, and software overhead, so the peak rating alone does not establish sustained performance. Under the illustrative 50% derating assumption, each 4 TOPS board sustains about 2 TOPS, so the target needs 5.2 ÷ 2 ≈ 2.6 boards, which rounds up to three. Multiple boards or a higher-tier accelerator remain candidates only if the model's operators and numerical format are supported. A multi-board design additionally requires divisible work and manageable coordination overhead; measurements of the actual model and runtime must establish sustained performance and task quality.

terms.def: Placing computation near the data when transfer delay or bandwidth makes remote execution infeasible.
